title: SoftBank's Son courting Gulf investors for a $100B operating-business AI fund
subtitle: The Financial Times reports early talks for a vehicle that would acquire traditional companies and remake them with AI software and robotics, with SoftBank's Roze unit at the center.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son is in early talks with Gulf investors — primarily in the United Arab Emirates — about a new vehicle targeting up to $100 billion to buy operating businesses and transform them with AI software and robotics, the Financial Times reported this week. The talks are preliminary, with no commitments and no final agreements described, and the FT noted there is no guarantee the discussions will result in a fund.

The strategy is a departure from SoftBank's earlier Vision Fund pattern. Instead of taking large minority stakes in AI developers, the proposed fund would acquire traditional companies — logistics, services, light manufacturing — and deploy AI and robotics to lift their margins. SoftBank's robotics unit Roze is expected to play a central operational role in the transformations, which is unusual for a private equity-style vehicle and shifts the risk from valuation calls on young AI companies to execution calls on mature-industry turnarounds.

The context is a familiar tension in SoftBank's portfolio. Son has committed heavily to OpenAI, including participation in its record funding rounds, while SoftBank's own share price has fallen sharply from its recent highs. The first Vision Fund's gains ($21.7 billion as of its last disclosure) have been largely offset by Vision Fund 2's losses ($22.9 billion as of June 2026). A $100 billion operating-business vehicle would reset the thesis — away from the model-training layer where OpenAI, Anthropic and Google already dominate, toward the much larger pool of companies that use AI as a cost input rather than a product.

A takeaway for learners: the next wave of AI value capture may not come from building models. It may come from pointing existing models at businesses that have been slow to adopt them. If you are weighing whether to join a frontier lab or an industrial operator trying to retrofit itself with AI, Son's bet is that the second category is where the leverage now sits — and he is backing it with real capital.
